{{short description|Polish-American mathematician}}
[[File:Nathan Altshiller Court.jpeg|thumb|right|Nathan Altshiller Court]]
'''Nathan Altshiller Court''' (January 22, 1881 – July 20, 1968) was a Polish–American mathematician. He was a [[geometry|geometer]] and the author of the popular book ''College Geometry'',{{r|eves}} who spent most of his career at the [[University of Oklahoma]].

==Biography==
Nathan A. Court was born Natan Altszyller{{r|name}} on 22 January 1881, in [[Warsaw]], [[Congress Poland|Russian Poland]], the eldest of nine children.{{r|goodman}} He attended primary and secondary school in Warsaw, but due to [[History of the Jews in Poland#Jews of Poland within the Russian Empire (1795–1918)|anti-Jewish discrimination]] could not attend university there.{{r|wiley}} In 1907 he moved to Belgium where he attended the [[University of Liège]] and the [[University of Ghent]], receiving his D.Sc. in 1911.{{r|wiley|goodman}}

Immediately afterward he moved to [[New York City]], anglicizing his name to Nathan Altshiller.{{r|wiley|djn}} Though he could not read or write in English when he arrived, within weeks he began lecturing in advanced mathematics at [[Columbia University]],{{r|wiley}} and at the beginning of the next semester he was hired as a mathematics instructor teaching evening classes while doing his graduate work in Mathematics and Astronomy during the day.{{r|levy}} In 1912 he married Sophie Ravitch, whom he had known in Warsaw.{{r|wiley}} He left New York in 1913, teaching for two years at the [[University of Washington]] in [[Seattle]] where his son Arnold was born in 1914, and for two years at the [[University of Colorado]].{{r|wiley}}

In 1916 he moved to the [[University of Oklahoma]], where he remained for the rest of his career.{{r|wiley|copanleader}} In 1919, he became a U.S. citizen and changed his last name to Court, keeping Altshiller as a middle name.{{r|ardmoreite|djn}} The first edition of his best known book, ''College Geometry'', a university-level textbook in [[synthetic geometry]], was published in 1925.{{r|cg-reviews}} In 1935 he published the [[solid geometry]] textbook ''Modern Pure Solid Geometry''{{r|mpsg-reviews}} and became a full professor at the University of Oklahoma. He continued teaching there until his retirement in 1951. ''College Geometry'' was continually in print without revision for over 25 years, but a revised edition was published in 1952.{{r|djn}} A collection of his essays, ''Mathematics in Fun and in Earnest'', was published in 1958.{{r|mfe-reviews}}

Court died  of heart attack in [[Norman, Oklahoma]] on 20 July 1968.{{r|levy}}

In his recognition, the Nathan A. Court Award was established by the OU Department of Mathematics, given to an outstanding freshman or sophomore math major.<ref>[https://www.ou.edu/cas/math/awards/2020/court Nathan A. Court Award] </ref>

== Works ==

* [https://archive.org/details/collegegeometryi00alts ''College Geometry: An Introduction to the Modern Geometry of the Triangle and the Circle''], 2nd ed., Barnes & Noble, 1952 [1st ed. 1925]
* [https://archive.org/details/modernpuresolidg0000nath ''Modern Pure Solid Geometry''], Macmillan, 1935
* [https://archive.org/details/mathematicsinfun0000alts/ ''Mathematics in Fun and in Earnest''], Dial Press, 1958

Court wrote over 100 scholarly papers.{{r|goodman|kimberling}} He was a frequent contributor to ''[[The American Mathematical Monthly]]''{{'}}s problem section.{{r|eves}}
